r: This gateway course orients physical education teaching majors to the profession: the history of the field, the sequence of Colorado licensure steps, professional dispositions such as punctuality, initiative, and response to feedback, and drafting standards-aligned lesson and unit plans. The lesson- and unit-plan drafting sits inside writing and organizational tasks that observed-usage data show AI already performs competently, so part of the applied output is exposed even now. But the course is also the required entry point into a board-approved PE teacher-licensure sequence -- every later PETE methods course lists it as prerequisite -- giving it a strong foundational role that a single semester of AI-drafted plans does not replace. Coaching professional dispositions is evaluative and interpersonal in a way automation does not substitute for. At 24 months, diffusion into teacher-prep advising is still limited, so the instrumental need for this specific gateway course remains largely intact.

By 2031, AI tools will draft competent standards-aligned lesson and unit plans on request, and much of the course's planning-template content becomes something a candidate could generate rather than construct from first principles -- pushing the planning-and-writing slice of the course toward Medium exposure. Task-exposure research places planning and drafting work among more-exposed activity categories, consistent with that shift. What resists erosion is the course's institutional position: as the required gateway into a licensure-gated preparation program whose curriculum a state board must approve, it remains a fixed requirement regardless of how AI-assisted the planning tasks become, and the professional-dispositions coaching still needs an instructor's real-time judgment. The rating moves to Medium at this horizon because the applied planning tasks are increasingly AI-competent even though the course's place in the required sequence is unchanged. Confidence is moderate given the course's mixed conceptual-and-orientation content.

Over a decade, AI-assisted lesson and unit planning should be routine in teacher preparation, and generating historically grounded overviews of the profession is well within model capability by any central-case capability trend. That keeps the planning-and-history content at Medium rather than pushing it higher, because the course's foundational role as prerequisite to the entire PETE sequence and its place inside a board-approved licensure program continue to require candidates to pass through it regardless of what tools they use once inside. The genuine uncertainty is how much of the dispositions coaching and licensure advising migrates into AI-assisted advising systems; that portion is harder to forecast than the planning content. The rating holds at Medium, reflecting that applied planning work is largely delegable while the gateway, foundational, and licensure functions of the course are not.
PETE 1601.d: The course will introduce the student to the professional preparation for the physical educator in the broadest sense. Thus, the students' experiences in the course will include learning about the history of physical education, being introduced to the steps for teacher licensure, learning of professional dispositions including attendance/punctuality, self-initiative, reliability, communication skills, and response to feedback. Important physical education concepts will be covered including; standards, objectives, lesson plan design, as well as unit planning. Students will learn how to use campus resources important to their success as students.

r: Methods of Teaching Outdoor Education trains PE candidates to lead adventure and outdoor-education activities across seasons: instructing groups in physical outdoor skills, managing group safety in variable terrain, and adapting activities to weather and setting. This is embodied, in-person, real-time work with elevated safety stakes -- exactly the manual, physically-present category that task-exposure research finds least exposed to AI. No model leads a group through a ropes course, teaches orienteering in the field, or reads a group's fatigue and risk level in real time. The course contributes to a licensure-gated K-12 PE preparation program's methods requirements, a program-level mandate even though this specific course is not individually named by statute. At 24 months the instrumental need to physically practice leading outdoor activities is untouched; AI is simply not the operative variable for this embodied competence.

By 2031, AI planning tools may help generate seasonal activity sequences or risk-management checklists, a modest augmentation of the course's administrative edges. That does not reach the core competence: leading real people through physical outdoor activity, reading environmental and group conditions, and intervening for safety in real time remain squarely embodied tasks outside AI's operative range. Verification burden reinforces this -- a misjudged outdoor safety call has real physical consequences, so a knowledgeable, present human is required regardless of what planning software exists. The program-level licensure mandate for PE methods coursework across activity domains persists on an institutional timeline slower than a single catalog cycle. The rating holds Low: capability growth in adjacent planning tasks does not touch the field-leadership skill this course develops, and the hedge widens only around how much administrative support AI provides instructors.

A decade of capability growth, even under an aggressive central-case scenario, does not plausibly produce a system that leads a group of K-12 students through embodied outdoor and adventure activities in real physical settings; the psychomotor, real-time, safety-critical nature of the work is categorically resistant to the current trajectory of AI capability, however fast task-time horizons are expanding elsewhere. The program-level requirement that PE licensure candidates demonstrate competence across activity domains including outdoor education also shows no plausible path to relaxation by 2036. The genuine uncertainty at this horizon concerns how much AI mediates trip planning, logistics, or risk documentation around the activity, not whether the embodied instructional competence itself is still required. The rating remains Low with high confidence, anchored by embodiment and by the program's persistent methods requirement.
PETE 1665.d: This course is intended for K-12 Physical Education teaching majors and covers outdoor education experiences and methodology. Topics will include an array of outdoor and adventure education activities throughout various seasons.

r: This course acquaints K-12 PE majors with the theories, rationale, activities, and materials used to teach physical activities and rhythms to elementary-age children -- a blend of curriculum theory (exposed, writing-adjacent) and applied activity content taught and practiced with children's movement development in mind (embodied, presence-dependent). Task-exposure research finds curriculum-rationale writing and materials synthesis more automatable than the applied side, where an instructor must model movement, read a child's developmental readiness, and adjust instruction live. That embodied core keeps the rating protected even as AI increasingly drafts curricular rationale competently. The program-level PE licensure mandate requiring elementary movement-content methods coursework, though not naming this exact course by statute, adds institutional weight. At 24 months the applied, child-facing teaching competence the course builds is largely intact, with only the curriculum-writing slice meaningfully touched by AI.

By 2031, AI drafting of curriculum rationale, activity progressions, and materials lists will be markedly more capable, and a candidate could plausibly generate a serviceable elementary movement unit with AI assistance. Jagged-frontier findings caution, however, that AI users outside a system's competence frontier perform worse with misplaced confidence -- and judging developmentally appropriate movement sequencing for young children sits closer to that frontier edge than routine writing does, sustaining real verification burden. The embodied instructional half of the course, demonstrating and adapting rhythms and movement activities with children present, remains outside AI's operative range regardless of drafting gains. The program-level methods mandate persists on an institutional clock slower than five years. The rating stays Low, dampened by embodiment and verification burden even as the conceptual planning content becomes more AI-assisted.

Over a decade, AI-generated elementary movement curricula and rationale documents should be routine and largely serviceable, meaningfully eroding the course's knowledge-transmission function around theory and materials selection. What remains resistant is the applied competence of teaching movement and rhythm activities to real children -- an embodied, developmentally sensitive, presence-dependent skill -- and the licensure program's continuing requirement that PE candidates demonstrate elementary movement-methods competence. The uncertainty widens considerably at this horizon: it is plausible curricular planning shifts almost entirely to AI-assisted workflows while the practicum-style teaching component remains fully human. Given that mix, and without a clear central-case path to removing the embodied instructional requirement, the rating holds Low rather than rising, though with less confidence than at nearer horizons given how much curriculum-development work could migrate to AI tools.
PETE 1670.d: This course is intended for K-12 Physical Education teaching majors. It is a course designed to acquaint students with theories, rationale, activities and materials used to teach physical activities and rhythms to children at the elementary school level.

r: This course acquaints K-12 PE majors with the theories, rationales, activities, and materials used to teach physical activities to secondary-age students, the mirror of the elementary curriculum course at an adolescent developmental level. As with its elementary counterpart, curriculum rationale and materials synthesis are writing-adjacent tasks that task-exposure research treats as more exposed, while the applied competence of demonstrating activities, managing adolescent classes, and adapting instruction to teenage physical and social development is embodied and presence-dependent. Secondary PE also carries heightened classroom-management and safety stakes given older students' physical capability, sustaining verification burden. The program-level PE licensure mandate for secondary movement-content methods coursework applies here without naming this exact course by statute. At 24 months, the applied, adolescent-facing teaching competence remains largely untouched, with AI meaningfully assisting only the curricular-writing component.

By 2031, drafting secondary PE curriculum rationale and unit materials with AI assistance will be commonplace, and that slice of the course's content becomes something a candidate generates rather than builds from scratch. Jagged-frontier research is relevant here: sequencing developmentally appropriate secondary activities and managing adolescent classroom dynamics sit closer to AI's competence edge than routine writing, so misplaced confidence in AI-generated curricular choices carries real risk, keeping verification burden meaningful. The embodied instructional core -- demonstrating activities, reading a secondary class's engagement and safety in real time -- remains outside AI's operative range. The licensure program's methods requirement persists on an institutional timeline slower than a single catalog cycle. The rating stays Low, dampened by embodiment and classroom verification demands even as curriculum drafting becomes increasingly AI-assisted.

A decade out, AI-generated secondary PE curricula and rationale should be routine and broadly competent, substantially eroding the course's original function of teaching candidates to construct such materials from first principles. The applied, in-person competence of teaching physical activities to adolescents and managing a secondary PE classroom remains resistant, and the licensure program's requirement that candidates demonstrate secondary movement-methods competence shows no clear path to removal by 2036 in the central case. The forecast is genuinely uncertain regarding how much of the curriculum-planning work shifts to AI-assisted workflows versus how much instructors still construct independently for accreditation or portfolio purposes. Given the embodied teaching core and the persistent program mandate, the rating holds Low, though with reduced confidence given how substantially the conceptual planning content could be displaced by then.
PETE 1680.d: This course is intended for K-12 Physical Education teaching majors. The course is designed to acquaint students with theories, rationales, activities and materials used to teach physical activities to students at the secondary school level.

r: Methods of Teaching Team Activities develops the applied teaching skills, strategies, and presentation techniques K-12 PE candidates need to instruct team sports, alongside performance analysis, classroom management, and real-time feedback delivery. Demonstrating skills, running drills, managing a gymnasium full of students, and giving live corrective feedback are embodied, in-person, real-time interpersonal tasks -- the category task-exposure research consistently finds least automatable, in contrast to the writing and coding tasks AI handles well. No model demonstrates a defensive stance or reads a class's engagement and safety in a live gym setting. The course sits inside a licensure-gated PE preparation program's methods requirement across activity domains, a program-level institutional mandate. At 24 months the instrumental need to physically practice teaching team activities in person is essentially untouched; capability growth elsewhere does not reach this competence.

By 2031, AI video-analysis tools may assist with performance-analysis feedback -- flagging technique errors from recorded footage -- offering modest augmentation to one component of the course. That leaves the core applied competence unchanged: leading live team-activity instruction, managing a class of moving students, and delivering real-time corrective feedback remain embodied, presence-dependent tasks outside AI's operative range, and the verification burden of classroom and physical safety keeps a trained human necessary regardless of analytic tools available. The program-level licensure mandate requiring team-activity methods coursework persists on an institutional clock slower than a single catalog cycle. The rating holds Low: the analytic edges of performance feedback see modest AI assistance, but the instrumental case for practicing embodied instruction in person is preserved by embodiment and the licensure structure together.

Even under a central-case decade of rapid capability growth, leading live team-activity instruction for K-12 students -- demonstrating skills, managing group dynamics, and making real-time safety and pedagogical judgments in a gymnasium or field -- remains outside what AI performs on a candidate's behalf; embodiment is the defining constraint, not the current pace of capability improvement. The PE licensure program's methods requirement across activity domains, including team sports pedagogy, shows no plausible route to elimination by 2036 in the central case. The most likely change is in how much AI-assisted video analytics augments the performance-feedback component, not in whether candidates must practice live instructional delivery. The rating remains Low with high confidence, reflecting that this is among the more durably protected courses in the catalog by embodiment and institutional structure combined.
PETE 2010.d: This course covers various methodologies of teaching team activities for the K-12 Physical Education major. It is designed to develop the teaching skills, strategies, and presentation techniques necessary to effectively teach a variety of team activities. Students will also learn the skills associated with performance analysis, classroom management, and teacher feedback as they relate to team activities.

r: Teaching Weight Training and Fitness Education develops the skills, strategies, and presentation techniques needed to instruct weight training and fitness principles, alongside exercise prescription, exercise testing, and fitness-testing administration. The prescription and testing-protocol elements draw on structured, rules-based content that consumer fitness apps and AI systems already assist with, giving this course modestly higher automatable content than a pure activity-teaching course. But the applied instructional core -- physically demonstrating lifts, spotting for safety, correcting form in real time, and administering fitness tests hands-on -- is embodied and presence-dependent, and errors in spotting or form correction carry real injury risk, sustaining verification burden. The course also sits inside the PE licensure program's activity-methods requirement. At 24 months the embodied teaching and safety-supervision core keeps the instrumental need largely intact despite AI-assisted prescription tools entering the fitness space.

By 2031, AI-generated exercise prescriptions and fitness-testing protocols will be common and competent, consistent with productivity research showing AI tools deliver meaningful task-speed gains on structured, rules-based work -- pushing the prescription-design slice of the course toward greater exposure. That does not reach the physically supervised core: spotting a lifter, correcting form in real time, and safely administering hands-on fitness tests remain embodied tasks where verification burden is real, since a missed safety cue has direct physical consequences for the student being spotted. The licensure program's methods requirement for fitness-content pedagogy persists on an institutional timeline slower than five years and is not tied to how automated the prescription side of the field becomes. The rating stays Low, dampened jointly by embodiment and by safety-verification demands, even as the algorithmic side of exercise prescription becomes substantially AI-assisted in commercial and school settings alike.

A decade out, AI-driven exercise-prescription and fitness-testing software should be pervasive in both commercial and school settings, substantially automating the algorithmic planning content this course teaches. The applied, embodied competence of physically instructing and safety-supervising weight training and fitness activities in person remains resistant, since spotting and hands-on correction are not tasks a model performs for the learner, and the PE licensure program's fitness-methods requirement shows no clear path to removal by 2036 in the central case. The genuine uncertainty concerns how much prescription and testing-protocol content the course still teaches manually versus through AI-assisted tools by then. Given the persistent embodied-safety core and institutional mandate, the rating holds Low, though with moderate rather than high confidence given how much the algorithmic component could shrink.
PETE 2030.d: This course covers methods of teaching weight training and physical fitness for the K-12 Physical Education major. It is designed to develop the skills, strategies and presentation techniques necessary to effectively teach the principles of weight training and fitness education in a physical activity and/or classroom setting. Students will also learn the skills associated with exercise prescription, exercise testing, and fitness testing administration.

r: Methods of Teaching Individual/Dual Activities, Level I develops the teaching skills, strategies, and presentation techniques K-12 PE candidates need to instruct individual and dual activities such as racquet or target sports, along with performance analysis, classroom management, and live feedback delivery. As with the team-activities methods course, the applied core is embodied and real-time: demonstrating technique, running drills for pairs or individuals, and correcting form in person are tasks squarely inside the physically-present, interpersonal category task-exposure research finds least exposed to AI. No model steps onto a court to demonstrate a serve or reads a student's mechanics live. The course fulfills part of the PE licensure program's activity-methods requirement, a program-level institutional mandate spanning multiple activity domains. At 24 months the instrumental need to physically practice this embodied instruction is essentially untouched.

By 2031, AI video-analysis tools may offer modest assistance with performance-analysis feedback on recorded individual or dual-activity technique, similar to the team-activities case. That leaves the applied instructional core unchanged: leading live individual and dual-activity instruction, managing pairs of students, and delivering real-time technique correction remain embodied, presence-dependent tasks outside AI's operative range. Verification burden from classroom and physical safety keeps a trained human necessary regardless of what analytic tools assist the feedback loop. The licensure program's methods mandate for individual and dual-activity pedagogy persists across an institutional timeline slower than a single catalog cycle. The rating holds Low: modest augmentation at the analytic margins does not touch the embodied core, and the licensure structure adds a second layer of protection.

Even under an aggressive central-case decade of capability growth, leading live individual- and dual-activity instruction -- demonstrating technique, pairing and managing students, and making real-time safety and pedagogical judgments on a court or field -- is not a task AI performs on a candidate's behalf; the constraint is embodiment, not the pace of model improvement. The PE licensure program's requirement that candidates demonstrate methods competence across individual and dual activity domains shows no plausible route to removal by 2036 in the central case. The most likely decade-scale change is in how much AI-assisted video analytics support the performance-feedback component, not in whether embodied instructional practice remains required. The rating stays Low with high confidence, among the more durably protected courses in the catalog.
PETE 2040.d: This course covers various methodologies of teaching individual and dual activities for the K-12 Physical Education major. It is designed to develop the teaching skills, strategies, and presentation techniques necessary to effectively teach a variety of the selected activities. Students will also learn the skills associated with performance analysis, classroom management, and teacher feedback as it relates to individual/dual activities.

r: Methods of Teaching Individual/Dual Activities, Level II builds on Level I with skill themes, movement concepts, and advanced locomotor and manipulative skills, adding explicit focus on teaching styles and pedagogical concepts for diversity and exceptionality -- adapting instruction for culture, race, gender, and physical, emotional, mental, and developmental differences. The activity-teaching core remains embodied and presence-dependent like its Level I counterpart, resisting automation for the same reasons. The differentiated-instruction content adds a layer of interpretive, high-stakes judgment about individual students' needs -- exactly the adversarial, non-obvious-failure-mode territory where verification burden is highest and a knowledgeable human is required. The course fulfills part of the PE licensure program's activity-methods requirement. At 24 months, both the embodied instructional core and the sensitive adaptive-pedagogy content keep the instrumental need for this course fully intact.

By 2031, AI may assist candidates in surfacing general strategies for adapting instruction to disability or cultural difference, a modest augmentation to the theoretical component. Jagged-frontier research is directly relevant to the exceptionality content: applying general adaptive-pedagogy suggestions to a specific student's needs sits outside AI's reliable competence frontier, and misplaced confidence in generic recommendations carries real equity and safety risk for vulnerable learners, sustaining high verification burden. The embodied activity-instruction core remains outside AI's operative range for the same reasons as Level I. The licensure program's methods mandate covering diversity and exceptionality content persists on an institutional timeline slower than five years. The rating holds Low, protected jointly by embodiment and by the elevated verification demands of adaptive pedagogy for diverse and exceptional learners.

A decade out, embodied instruction of individual and dual activities remains resistant to AI substitution for the same durable reasons as at nearer horizons, and the course's differentiated-pedagogy content -- teaching styles responsive to culture, gender, and exceptionality -- retains meaningful verification burden even as general AI capability grows, because applying adaptive strategies correctly to individual students in real classrooms carries real consequences for vulnerable learners that a general model cannot be trusted to judge unsupervised. The PE licensure program's requirement for this content shows no clear path to relaxation by 2036 in the central case. The genuine uncertainty concerns how much AI-generated background knowledge about exceptionality and cultural responsiveness supplements candidate preparation, not whether the applied, judgment-laden teaching competence itself is still required. The rating holds Low with moderate-to-high confidence.
PETE 2090.d: This course covers various methodologies of teaching individual and dual activities for the K-12 Physical Education major. The students will learn skill themes, movement concepts, and advanced locomotor and manipulative skills as they relate to individual/dual activities. Additionally, this class will focus on teaching styles and pedagogical concepts important to diversity (culture, race, gender, etc) and exceptionality (physical, emotional, mental and developmental abilities).

r: Health and Physical Education for Elementary Teachers gives prospective early-childhood and elementary generalists a basic background in school health and PE content -- not PE-major methods training, but a content-survey course preparing non-specialist teachers to deliver elementary health and PE material. This is knowledge-transmission work: learning what age-appropriate health and PE content exists and how to explain it, tasks closer to the writing and summarization category observed-usage data shows AI already performing competently, rather than the hands-on activity-instruction core of the PETE methods sequence. The course still contributes to elementary teacher licensure content requirements, a program-level mandate, though it is not itself a hard clinical or field-specific requirement and is more terminal in the curriculum than foundational. At 24 months, the course's basic-content-survey nature leaves meaningful, if partial, exposure to AI-assisted content delivery.

By 2031, AI tools should competently generate age-appropriate health and PE content summaries and explain core concepts to a prospective elementary teacher on demand, consistent with task-exposure research finding explanatory and writing-adjacent knowledge work substantially exposed. The rating rises to Medium at this horizon because the course's content-survey function is increasingly something a model can deliver directly, and no embodiment or hard licensure lock specific to this course holds it back the way the PETE-major methods sequence is held back. What remains is the program-level requirement that elementary teacher candidates demonstrate competence in this content area, and the practical judgment of translating content into classroom-appropriate lessons, keeping the rating from rising further. The hedge widens here given genuine uncertainty about how elementary licensure programs will restructure content-survey requirements as AI content delivery becomes ordinary.

A decade out, AI-generated health and PE content explanation for prospective elementary teachers should be routine and reliable, and the course's core knowledge-transmission function is substantially eroded in instrumental terms. The rating holds at Medium rather than rising further because the program-level requirement that elementary licensure candidates cover this content area persists, and translating general content knowledge into actual classroom delivery for young children retains some practical, presence-dependent judgment the course also develops. The forecast is meaningfully uncertain at this horizon: elementary teacher-prep programs could restructure this requirement around AI-assisted content delivery well before 2036, or could preserve it largely unchanged given how foundational basic health and PE literacy is considered for generalist teachers. The rating reflects that balance rather than a confident point prediction.
PETE 2130.d: This course provides prospective early childhood and elementary teachers with a basic background in elementary school health and physical education programs. Students will learn the health and physical education content appropriate for elementary school children.

r: School Health Education examines the determinants and barriers of child and adolescent health, the knowledge, attitudes, and skills tied to behavior change, and the Coordinated School Health framework, with candidates implementing active-learning health lesson strategies. Much of this is conceptual and curricular -- researching health determinants, designing behavior-change lessons, structuring coordinated-health frameworks -- work that leans toward the writing and synthesis tasks observed-usage data shows AI increasingly performs well, more than the physically embodied activity-teaching courses elsewhere in the PETE sequence. What resists automation is delivering active-learning lessons live to real students and judging how a specific class responds to sensitive health topics, a presence-dependent instructional skill. The course also contributes to the PE licensure program's health-education content requirement. At 24 months, limited classroom diffusion of AI lesson-delivery tools keeps the instrumental need largely intact despite the exposed planning content.

By 2031, AI-assisted drafting of health lesson plans, behavior-change curricula, and Coordinated School Health documentation should be commonplace, consistent with task-exposure research placing curriculum and explanatory writing among more-exposed categories. That pushes the rating to Medium at this horizon: the planning and content-synthesis work that dominates much of the course description becomes substantially AI-assisted, even though delivering active-learning health lessons to real K-12 students in person, and navigating sensitive topics like behavior change with a live class, remains a presence-dependent skill requiring a trained instructor. The PE licensure program's health-content requirement persists on an institutional clock slower than five years, but it no longer fully protects the course given how much of its content is curricular rather than embodied-activity based. The hedge here reflects real uncertainty about classroom AI diffusion rates.

A decade out, AI-generated health curricula, determinant analyses, and behavior-change lesson frameworks should be routine and broadly competent, substantially eroding the course's original knowledge-construction function; the rating's upward pressure toward High is real. It is held at Medium because delivering active-learning health lessons to real students, judging classroom response to sensitive health and behavior topics, and coordinating school-health efforts across a real school community remain presence-dependent tasks that a model does not perform on the instructor's behalf, and the PE licensure program's health-content requirement shows no clear path to removal by 2036 in the central case. The genuine uncertainty is whether the balance tips further toward High if AI-mediated health instruction becomes normalized in K-12 settings faster than the central case assumes. The rating reflects that unresolved tension rather than a confident point estimate.
PETE 3000.d: School Health Education examines the determinants and barriers of health that impact children and adolescents. Knowledge, attitude and skill associated with behavior change are emphasized. Understanding the components of Coordinated School Health in creating a healthy school environment is also covered. Students will implement effective teaching strategies to create active- learning health lessons.

r: This companion course converts School of Education theory into standards-based instruction: drafting assessment management plans and curriculum projects, then micro-teaching lessons tied to Colorado Teacher Quality Standards and designing classroom-management approaches. The planning artifacts map to writing and documentation activities that task-exposure research classifies as positively exposed, and AI already drafts standards-aligned lesson outlines competently. But the course's core deliverable is live micro-teaching and collaborative lesson design with peers, a presence-dependent performance task outside that exposed slice. The binding constraint is programmatic: this is a required companion within Colorado's licensure-gated teacher-preparation sequence, though it carries no independent clinical clock hours itself. At 24 months, realized automation of the planning paperwork is real but partial, and the delivered-teaching component keeps the instrumental need for the course largely intact.

By 2031, AI drafting of standards-aligned lesson plans, assessment management templates, and interdisciplinary curriculum outlines will be materially more capable and more diffused into teacher-preparation coursework, consistent with observed-usage data showing writing and planning tasks concentrated in AI's most-used categories. That erodes the instrumental case for practicing the paperwork side of this course. What resists automation is the micro-teaching performance itself and the classroom-management judgment candidates must demonstrate under Colorado Teacher Quality Standards, which still requires direct observation and live feedback. The program mandate holds the course in the sequence, capping the rating at Medium rather than releasing it further. The trajectory reflects planning tasks increasingly AI-assisted while the practiced teaching-performance core remains a candidate competency employers and evaluators expect to see demonstrated in person.

Over a decade, generative planning tools could handle most of the standards-alignment and curriculum-documentation work this course currently teaches through guided assignments, and diffusion into teacher-education programs is plausible given the capability trend of rapidly lengthening AI task-time horizons. Even so, licensure programs are likely to keep requiring candidates to demonstrate the practiced act of micro-teaching and classroom-management design themselves, since evaluators assess candidate performance, not AI output, against Teacher Quality Standards. The rating holds at Medium, reflecting substantial erosion of the planning-artifact rationale alongside persistence of the applied-teaching-practice rationale. Genuine uncertainty remains about how far teacher-prep programs will lean on AI-assisted lesson design before requiring students to demonstrate unaided planning competence; this cuts against a confident further rise. The wide uncertainty band on this horizon concerns how much of the planning workload shifts, not whether candidates must still show they can teach a live lesson.
PETE 3010.d: This course is a companion course to and must be taken concurrently with PETE 3000. The course converts content, theory, and conceptual aspects of academic and professional teacher education into standards-based instruction through assignments, assessments management plans, and curriculum projects. Students plan and micro-teach lessons integrating Colorado Teacher Quality Standards and collaborate to develop interdisciplinary lessons. Students design a variety of models of instruction and approaches to classroom management to support learner's growth toward Quality Standards for Colorado teachers.

r: Candidates investigate developmental psychology, educational philosophy, social policy, and school governance to articulate a personal educational philosophy and design learning experiences grounded in theory. The applied work is almost entirely textual and discursive — synthesizing readings, constructing arguments, drafting learning designs — activities observed-usage data places squarely in AI's heaviest-used categories, and current models already produce competent philosophy-of-education essays. There is no embodiment protecting the task here. The binding constraint at this horizon is programmatic: admission to the School of Education is a prerequisite, and the course is a required foundational component of Colorado's licensure-gated teacher-preparation curriculum, which caps realized substitution regardless of how automatable the writing is. At 24 months, capability outpaces the institutional requirement that candidates personally produce this reasoning.

By 2031, AI will competently explain developmental-psychology and educational-philosophy frameworks and draft theory-grounded learning designs, consistent with task-exposure research's finding that writing-heavy knowledge work is strongly positively associated with automation exposure. The four essential questions the course poses — why schooling exists, how people learn, who decides curriculum, what teachers do — are the kind of synthesis task language models already handle competently, and diffusion into teacher-education coursework is plausible on this horizon. What keeps the rating from rising further is the program mandate: this remains a required foundations course inside the accredited licensure sequence, and evaluators still expect candidates to demonstrate their own reasoning. The rating moves to Medium as the knowledge-delivery rationale substantially erodes while the mandate persists.

A decade out, AI performing literature synthesis and theory application at this level is a reasonable central-case expectation, and the course's knowledge-transmission function is substantially eroded on capability grounds alone. Whether Colorado's teacher-licensure requirements or CAEP-aligned program design would relax the requirement that candidates personally construct an educational philosophy is far less certain — programmatic and accreditation change moves on a slower clock than model capability. The rating holds at Medium, reflecting real erosion of the underlying task alongside a persistent, if not absolute, institutional expectation that teacher candidates demonstrate this reasoning themselves. The wide uncertainty band applies to how licensure programs redesign assessment around AI-assisted writing, not to whether the underlying content knowledge remains teachable by AI. That said, capability trend research on rapidly lengthening AI task-time horizons suggests the underlying skill gap will keep narrowing regardless of how quickly programs adapt their assessments.
PETE 3130.d: Teacher candidates in this course will explore psychological and philosophical theories of education as they apply to secondary classrooms. Candidates will investigate four questions essential to future teachers: 1) Why do we have schooling? 2) How do people learn? 3) Who decides what and how students are taught? and 4) What do teachers do? Candidates address these questions by making connections between the fields of developmental psychology, educational philosophy, social policy, and school governance. Teacher candidates will demonstrate their understanding of these essential questions by articulating their educational philosophy and creating learning designs grounded in theory and best practices. This course - informed by current research on cognition, motivation, and culture - is designed to promote a deeper understanding of the rewards and challenges associated with becoming an effective teacher.

r: This course builds anatomical, biomechanical, and exercise-physiology knowledge and applies it in lecture and lab to analyze movement technique for K-12 physical-education curriculum. The knowledge component — recalling physiological mechanisms, explaining biomechanical principles — is the kind of factual synthesis current models handle well, but task-exposure research finds science and applied critical-thinking skills negatively associated with automation exposure relative to pure writing tasks, and the lab requires hands-on observation of live movement technique. That embodied technique-analysis work is not something a model performs on the student's behalf. The course also functions as content-knowledge substrate for later PETE methods and assessment courses, a foundational-scaffolding role that independently protects it. At 24 months, the instrumental need to build this applied science base through direct lab practice remains largely intact.

By 2031, AI tools will more capably explain biomechanical and physiological concepts and could plausibly assist in analyzing video of movement technique, meaningfully augmenting how the lecture portion of this course is taught — an instance of the jagged frontier where AI performs well on well-specified analytical sub-tasks. But directly observing, correcting, and teaching K-12-applicable movement technique in a live lab setting is not delegable, and the course continues to underpin later methods and adapted-PE coursework that assumes this movement-science foundation. The rating moves to Medium: the explanatory-knowledge layer becomes substantially AI-assisted, while the embodied lab-analysis core and the course's prerequisite role for the rest of the PETE sequence keep full substitution out of reach. Diffusion of such tools into physical-education teacher-preparation labs specifically remains uneven and slower than raw capability growth would suggest.

Over a decade, capability growth described by the METR/Epoch task-time-horizon trend could bring AI-assisted movement analysis — pose estimation, biomechanical modeling from video — into standard use for technique feedback, further eroding the lecture-content rationale for the course. Whether physical-education teacher-preparation programs would then treat hands-on lab competency as optional is a separate and much less certain question; foundational scaffolding for a teaching license built on demonstrated movement-science understanding is unlikely to disappear on a ten-year horizon. The rating holds Medium, hedged by real uncertainty about how much of the technique-analysis task migrates to automated tools versus how much programs continue to require direct student practice in identifying and correcting live movement. Programs are more likely to reallocate time toward interpreting automated technique feedback than to eliminate the supervised lab practice that builds a candidate's own diagnostic eye.
PETE 3200.d: Movement Science includes basic knowledge in anatomical, biomechanics, kinesiology, physiology, and exercise physiology as it applies to the practice of physical activity, fitness, and exercise in K-12 Physical Education. The course will apply movement concepts to analyze technique as it applies to K-12 Physical Education curriculum during lecture and lab portions of the class.

r: Taken concurrently with the PETE 3410 field placement, this course converts teacher-education theory into standards-based instruction through assignments, assessments, management plans, and teacher work samples, with candidates micro-teaching lessons integrating Colorado Teacher Quality Standards. The documentation-heavy tasks — assessment plans, work samples, interdisciplinary lesson design — sit in the writing and planning categories task-exposure research finds positively associated with AI exposure, and current models already draft usable lesson-plan scaffolds. The micro-teaching and classroom-management-design components remain presence-dependent, though. The binding constraint is the licensure-gated teacher-preparation sequence this course belongs to; it is a required methods course even though it carries no independent clinical clock hours. At 24 months, planning-task assistance is real but the demonstrated teaching performance keeps the course's instrumental need substantially intact.

By 2031, generating standards-aligned secondary PE lesson plans, management plans, and teacher work samples will likely be handled competently by AI, echoing productivity research showing large quality and speed gains on structured professional-writing tasks when AI assists lower-skill performers. That substantially automates the paperwork rationale for the course. The micro-teaching and interdisciplinary collaboration components, evaluated through live observation against Teacher Quality Standards, resist that substitution, and the program continues to require this methods course as a companion to supervised field experience. The rating rises to Medium: the drafting work that once justified extensive practice is increasingly AI-assisted, while the applied teaching-performance requirement and the program mandate keep the course from further erosion at this horizon. Diffusion into actual teacher-preparation classrooms, however, still lags what the underlying models can already do, tempering how far this shift has actually progressed by 2031.

A decade out, AI-assisted lesson planning and work-sample generation could become close to default practice in teacher-preparation programs if diffusion follows capability, substantially eroding the rationale for extensive graded practice on planning documents. Whether Colorado's licensure structure and its Teacher Quality Standards evaluation would still require candidates to personally demonstrate secondary PE methods through live micro-teaching is the harder, more durable question, and the central case keeps that requirement in place through 2036. The rating holds Medium, reflecting substantial erosion of the documentation-practice function alongside persistence of the practiced-teaching-performance function that the course and its program mandate are built around. Confidence narrows here given how much program design could shift in ten years. The wider uncertainty concerns exactly how licensure evaluators redesign teacher work-sample requirements around AI-assisted drafting, not whether live micro-teaching itself remains a required demonstration.
PETE 3400.d: This course is a companion course to and must be taken concurrently with PETE 3410. The course teaches students how to convert content, theory, and conceptual aspects of academic and professional teacher education into standards-based instruction through assignments, assessments, management plans, and teacher work samples. Students plan and micro-teach lessons integrating Colorado Teacher Quality Standards and collaborate to develop interdisciplinary lessons. Students design a variety of models of instruction and approaches to classroom management to support learner's growth toward Teacher Quality Standards for Colorado teachers.

r: This is a 60-hour field placement in a multicultural-dense secondary school, where candidates plan and teach lessons integrating Colorado and National PE Content Standards under a mentor teacher, engaging in culturally responsive teaching and real-time classroom management with actual adolescents. The applied task is in-person instructional delivery and interpersonal judgment with minors — the low-exposure, high-presence category task-exposure research consistently places outside AI's reach, regardless of how capable planning tools become. The binding constraint is a hard, course-specific mandate: Colorado's teacher-licensure pathway requires logged supervised field hours in a mentor-teacher setting that an AI system cannot satisfy. At 24 months, capability growth in lesson-planning assistance is irrelevant to whether a candidate must personally complete this clinical placement. Even the most capable lesson-planning assistant available at this horizon cannot log a single hour of the supervised classroom time the licensure pathway demands.

AI decision-support for lesson planning and formative assessment will be more common in K-12 classrooms by 2031, and candidates in this placement will likely work alongside such tools. That does not touch the requirement itself: the field hours must be earned through supervised, in-person teaching of real students under mentor observation, an embodied and presence-dependent activity with real child-welfare stakes that keep verification burden high. Colorado's field-hour mandate for secondary licensure operates on an institutional clock — roughly hundreds of hours across the secondary preparation sequence — that does not relax within one or two catalog cycles. The rating stays Low: whatever AI assists with in the classroom, the candidate must still be the one standing in front of students accumulating the mandated hours.

Even under a decade of substantial capability growth and broader classroom AI adoption, the structural requirement that secondary teacher candidates complete supervised in-person field hours with a mentor teacher is among the most durable constraints in the catalog; there is no credible central-case path to a licensure board eliminating it by 2036. The base automatability of the surrounding instructional-support tasks ticks up as AI handles more planning and data work, but the embodied, real-time, culturally responsive teaching performance this placement certifies is not the kind of task that gets delegated. The rating holds Low with high confidence. The open question is how heavily AI mediates what mentor teachers and candidates do inside those hours, not whether the hours themselves remain required.
PETE 3410.d: This course is a companion course to and must be taken concurrently with PETE 3400. The course allows students an opportunity in a multicultural population dense school to convert content, theory, and conceptual aspects of academic and professional teacher education into standards-based instruction through assignments, assessments, standards-based lesson planning, and engagement in a reflection cycle. Students plan and teach lessons integrating Colorado Teacher Quality Standards, Colorado and National Physical Education Content Standards with a mentor teacher. Students engage in culturally responsive teaching while designing a variety of models of instruction and approaches to classroom management to support learner's growth. They are in a guided environment under a mentor teacher while actively engaging in teacher practices and applying their content knowledge and pedagogical skills. This is a 60 hour field experience.

r: Candidates learn to design, administer, and interpret standards-based assessments across the psychomotor, cognitive, and affective domains in K-12 settings, then use results to monitor progress and structure instruction. Designing rubrics and analyzing assessment data are documentation and analysis tasks that observed-usage data places among AI's most common applications, and current tools already draft assessment instruments and summarize score patterns competently. But administering psychomotor assessments requires physically observing and rating live student movement, an embodied task outside that exposed slice, and grading decisions affecting real K-12 students carry meaningful stakes. There is no clinical clock-hour mandate on this specific course, only its contributory place in the licensure program. At 24 months, the design and analysis work is exposed but the applied administration keeps the course's instrumental need mostly intact.

By 2031, AI-assisted rubric design, item generation, and score-pattern analysis will likely be diffused into teacher-preparation assessment courses, though Census BTOS data shows firm-level AI adoption still uneven even as capability grows, so the pace of that diffusion into K-12 practice is not guaranteed. The psychomotor-domain administration piece — physically watching and scoring live student performance — remains resistant, and interpreting assessment results to make real instructional and grading decisions still carries a verification burden AI output alone doesn't satisfy. With no independent clinical mandate protecting this course, the rating moves to Medium: much of the design-and-analysis instruction becomes AI-assistable while the live-administration and decision-application core does not. The residual verification burden falls on interpreting what an assessment result means for a particular child's instructional next step, a judgment call the course is specifically built to teach.

A decade out, AI-generated assessment design and automated score analysis are plausible as standard classroom tools, further eroding the rationale for extensive practice building these artifacts by hand. Physically administering and rating psychomotor assessments with real K-12 students, and applying judgment about what results mean for individual learners, remains a demonstrated candidate competency that licensure programs are unlikely to treat as optional even a decade out. The rating holds Medium, reflecting substantial erosion of the design-and-analysis function without full erosion of the applied-administration function. The genuine uncertainty concerns how much of assessment interpretation itself migrates to automated dashboards before programs adjust what they require candidates to demonstrate unaided. The wider uncertainty concerns how much of that residual judgment eventually gets absorbed into automated instructional-recommendation systems, a shift that would only matter if verification norms in K-12 assessment relaxed alongside it.
PETE 3460.d: This course is designed to help students possess knowledge of standards-based assessment in psychomotor, cognitive, and affective domains and have skills of designing, administering, and interpreting assessments utilized in K-12 grade levels. Students will learn how to develop assessments and gather information to monitor student progress, structure effective lessons, and make grading more accurate and systematic.

r: This companion to the PETE 3510 field placement teaches candidates to convert teacher-education theory into standards-based elementary PE instruction through assignments, assessments, management plans, and teacher work samples, explicitly linking lessons to reading, technology, and mathematics. The interdisciplinary lesson-planning and work-sample documentation are writing-and-planning tasks that task-exposure research classifies as positively exposed, and AI already drafts serviceable cross-curricular lesson outlines. Micro-teaching delivery and classroom-management design for elementary learners remain presence-dependent and are evaluated through live observation. The course is a required methods component of Colorado's licensure-gated teacher-preparation sequence, though it carries no independent clock-hour mandate itself. At 24 months, the drafting-heavy assignments are increasingly AI-assistable while the demonstrated teaching practice keeps the course's core purpose substantially unautomated. Even fluent AI-drafted lesson plans still require a candidate to stand in front of elementary students and execute the lesson under observation.

By 2031, drafting standards-aligned elementary lesson plans, management plans, and cross-curricular work samples will likely be well within AI capability, consistent with productivity research showing large speed and quality gains on structured professional-writing tasks. That meaningfully erodes the instrumental case for the paperwork-practice side of the course. What remains resistant is micro-teaching performance and classroom-management judgment specific to elementary learners, assessed through direct observation against Colorado Teacher Quality Standards, and the program continues to require this methods course alongside supervised field experience. The rating moves to Medium: the planning-artifact rationale weakens substantially while the applied-teaching-demonstration rationale and the program mandate hold the floor. The residual instructional work — reading a room of young learners and adjusting a lesson in real time — is exactly the kind of live, presence-dependent judgment that current productivity research finds AI does not substitute for.

Over a decade, AI-assisted lesson and work-sample generation could become routine practice in elementary teacher-preparation coursework if diffusion tracks capability growth, further eroding the documentation-practice rationale. Whether the program would then also relax the expectation that candidates personally demonstrate elementary PE methods through live micro-teaching is a separate and less certain question tied to accreditation and licensure design rather than model capability, and the central case keeps that requirement through 2036. The rating holds Medium, reflecting substantial erosion of the planning-practice function while the practiced-teaching-performance function persists. Confidence is moderate given real uncertainty about how far programs let AI-assisted planning substitute for graded practice before requiring unaided demonstration. The wider uncertainty concerns how much programs lean on AI-assisted drafting as a starting point for candidate lesson plans rather than as a replacement for the graded practice itself.
PETE 3500.d: This course is a companion course to and must be taken concurrently with PETE 3510: Clinical Experience in Elementary Physical Education. The course teaches students how to convert content, theory and conceptual aspects of academic and professional teacher education into standards based instruction through assignments, assessments, management plans, and teacher work samples. Students plan and micro-teach lessons integrating Colorado Teacher Quality Standards and collaborate to develop interdisciplinary lessons that link physical education to reading, technology and mathematics. Students design a variety of models for instruction and approaches to classroom management to support learner's growth toward Colorado Teacher Quality Standards.

r: This 60-hour standards-based field experience places pre-student-teaching candidates in elementary school settings to demonstrate developing teaching competencies, implement and assess integrated lessons, and adjust instruction for diverse learners including students with special needs. The applied work is in-person instruction and real-time classroom management with actual elementary children — squarely in the low-exposure, high-presence category task-exposure research places outside AI's reach. The binding constraint is a hard, course-specific institutional mandate: Colorado's teacher-licensure pathway requires candidates to log supervised field hours in an actual elementary classroom, a requirement no AI system can fulfill regardless of its instructional-planning ability. At 24 months, the instrumental need for a candidate to personally complete this placement is fully intact; capability growth elsewhere is not the operative variable here.

By 2031, AI tools supporting lesson planning and formative assessment will likely be present in elementary classrooms, and candidates completing this placement may well use them. That leaves the requirement itself untouched: candidates must still demonstrate teaching competencies and manage diverse learners, including students with special needs, through direct in-person practice under supervision — a formative, presence-dependent experience with real child-welfare stakes that sustain high verification burden. Colorado's field-hour mandate for elementary licensure preparation does not shift within a catalog cycle or two; institutional change of this kind moves far slower than model capability. The rating stays Low: whatever assists inside the classroom, the candidate must still personally accumulate the mandated in-person hours. The verification burden here is inseparable from the placement's purpose: an evaluator must watch the candidate teach and manage real children to certify the competency at all.

A decade of AI capability growth and even broad classroom adoption does not plausibly remove the requirement that elementary teacher candidates complete supervised in-person field hours before advancing toward student teaching; this is among the most durable constraints in the catalog. The base rate of adjacent instructional-support automation rises over that horizon, but the embodied, interpersonal, and adaptive teaching practice this placement is designed to build and certify is not delegable to a model. The rating holds Low with high confidence given the licensure mandate. The genuine open question is how much AI mediates instructional planning and assessment inside those hours, not whether the hours and the personal, in-person teaching practice they require remain necessary. The wider uncertainty concerns how much AI mediates lesson content and data analysis during those hours, not whether a candidate must still personally stand in front of a class of children to earn them.
PETE 3510.d: This course is a companion course to and must be taken concurrently with PETE 3500: Methods of Teaching Elementary Physical Education. This course integrates the content, theory, and conceptual aspects of academic and professional teacher education in a 60-hour standards based field experience in elementary physical education. This field experience provides the pre-student teaching candidate opportunities in school settings to demonstrate their developing teaching competencies and extends opportunities to implement and assess integrated lessons that promote student achievement. Students apply principles of teaching and classroom management to make appropriate decisions for diverse groups of learners and to adjust approaches for elementary physical education students with special needs.

r: This course covers risk prevention, first aid and CPR, liability, supervision, and recognizing environmental risks, psychological disorders, medical conditions, and injuries specific to K-12 physical-education and general P-12 education settings. The informational content — liability frameworks, recognizing risk categories, decision protocols — is text-based knowledge AI already explains competently, positively exposed per task-exposure research. But CPR and first-aid competency require hands-on skill demonstration, and recognizing an emerging medical or psychological emergency in a live PE setting demands embodied, real-time judgment with a child's safety at stake, keeping verification burden high. The course serves both PE and general education majors as a shared program requirement rather than carrying its own clinical clock hours. At 24 months, the knowledge layer is exposed while the demonstrated safety-skill core keeps the course substantially necessary.

By 2031, AI will more capably deliver liability and risk-recognition content and could plausibly generate scenario-based training materials, an instance of the jagged frontier where structured informational tasks are well within AI's reach. Physically demonstrating CPR technique and correctly recognizing signs of injury or psychological distress in a live PE environment remains outside that frontier, and the real safety consequences of a missed or mishandled emergency keep a knowledgeable, competent human necessary. The course continues to serve as a shared requirement across PE and education programs without gaining or losing an independent licensure mandate. The rating moves to Medium: the explanatory content becomes largely AI-deliverable while the hands-on safety-skill demonstration anchors continued necessity. Verification here is not abstract — a missed sign of a concussion or an allergic reaction has immediate physical consequences, which is exactly the high-error-cost condition that keeps a trained human necessary.

Over a decade, AI-generated risk-scenario training and liability guidance could become a standard supplement to how this content is taught, further eroding the knowledge-delivery rationale. Whether teacher-preparation and PE programs would then also drop the requirement that candidates personally demonstrate CPR and first-aid competency and practice recognizing live emergencies is a separate, much less likely shift — professional safety-certification norms outside AI's control typically require hands-on demonstration regardless of available information tools. The rating holds Medium, reflecting substantial erosion of the informational-content function while the embodied safety-skill demonstration persists as the binding rationale. Confidence is moderate given uncertainty about how certification bodies might eventually treat simulation-based practice. The wider uncertainty concerns exactly how much simulation-based or AI-assisted scenario training substitutes for live practice sessions, not whether some form of hands-on skill verification remains required for licensure.
PETE 3800.d: This course is designed to provide K-12 physical education majors and P-12 education majors an overview of potential areas of risk faced by educators. Specifically, elements of risk prevention, first aid and CPR, assessment, and intervention are discussed as they apply within a school setting. Topics include: liability; decision making; supervision; protecting children; recognizing environmental risks; recognizing psychological disorders; recognizing general medical conditions; and, recognizing and evaluating common injuries related to physical education and activity.

r: This capstone methods course teaches candidates to include children with disabilities in general PE settings, covering disability characteristics and movement impact, IDEA-related legislation, assessment, Individualized Education Plans, and inclusion strategies. IEP-related documentation and legislative-compliance knowledge are text-based tasks observed-usage data places among AI's common applications, and models already summarize special-education law and draft accommodation language competently. But designing and delivering inclusive teaching strategies in a live PE setting with real students of varying abilities is presence-dependent, real-time instructional practice, and misjudging an accommodation carries genuine welfare stakes for a vulnerable learner. The course is a required licensure-program methods course without independent clinical clock hours. At 24 months, the compliance-knowledge layer is exposed while the applied inclusive-teaching practice keeps the course largely necessary.

By 2031, AI will likely draft IEP-aligned accommodations and summarize disability-specific movement considerations with real competence, consistent with observed-usage patterns showing AI concentrated in documentation and knowledge-retrieval tasks. That erodes the instrumental case for extensive practice on the compliance-and-documentation side of adapted PE. Delivering inclusive instruction to real students with disabilities in a general PE setting, adjusting in real time, and building the interpersonal trust such teaching requires remain outside that exposed slice, and the verification burden around vulnerable-student welfare stays elevated. No independent clinical mandate protects this specific course, but the licensure program continues to require it. The rating moves to Medium as the compliance-knowledge function is substantially automated while the applied inclusive-teaching function persists. The wider trend toward AI-assisted documentation does not touch the interpersonal skill of adapting instruction for a specific child's needs in the moment, which remains the course's central demonstrated competency.

A decade out, AI handling IEP documentation and disability-related compliance knowledge at expert level is a reasonable central case, further eroding the course's original knowledge-transmission rationale. Whether licensure programs would then treat live inclusive-teaching practice with students with disabilities as optional is far less likely, given the safety and welfare stakes involved and the persistent expectation that teacher candidates demonstrate this competency directly rather than through automated tools. The rating holds Medium, reflecting substantial erosion of the compliance-and-documentation layer alongside continued necessity of demonstrated inclusive-teaching skill. The uncertainty band widens at this horizon around how licensure programs restructure adapted-PE assessment, not around whether inclusive in-person teaching practice remains valuable to certify. The wider uncertainty concerns exactly how licensure programs redesign adapted-PE coursework around AI-assisted IEP support, not whether candidates must still demonstrate inclusive teaching with real students under supervision.
PETE 4620.d: This course is designed to give future teachers the skills and knowledge to effectively include children with disabilities in the general physical education setting or least restrictive environment. Course content includes characteristics of selected disabilities and how these disabilities impact a person's movement potential and performance, legislation, assessment, Individual Education Plans, strategies for inclusion and teaching methods in the physical education setting.
